content.title: About
content.content: Water, tonic is a non‑alcoholic beverage made by carbonating pure water and adding a small amount of flavorings, sugar or sweeteners, and sometimes a light bitterness (e.g., quinine). It is commonly used as a mixer in cocktails and as a refreshing drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tonic originated in India as a malaria remedy thanks to its quinine content.
Modern tonic usually contains only trace amounts of quinine, with sweetness provided by sugar or sweeteners.
Carbonated water was invented in the early 19th century and quickly became a popular base for tonics.
Tonic is often served over ice with a lime wedge, highlighting its refreshing character.
In some countries tonic is considered a "healthy" drink because of its small vitamin B content.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like plain water, tonic helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Mild digestive stimulation
items.content: The acidity and slight bitterness of quinine can promote gastric juice production.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Small amounts of quinine and certain flavorings possess antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low calorie (when sweetened with substitutes)
items.content: Diet versions of tonic can be a good alternative to sugary sodas.

items.title: Supports cocktail mixing
items.content: Tonic adds a bitter note that enhances the aroma of spirit‑based cocktails.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional tonic may contain significant sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Quinine interactions
items.content: People taking quinine‑sensitive medications (e.g., anticoagulants) should limit tonic consumption.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Some individuals experience stomach discomfort or heartburn from carbonated drinks.

items.title: Allergy to flavorings
items.content: Rarely, allergic reactions to added flavor compounds can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tonic can be enjoyed chilled, often with a slice of lime or lemon. It is widely used as a base for cocktails (e.g., gin‑tonic) and in cooking for marinades or desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the tonic bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep it refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.
